\chapter*{Devanagari --- a reference}
\addcontentsline{toc}{chapter}{Devanagari (reference)}
\markboth{Devanagari}{Devanagari}

A \textbf{reference}, not a chapter — a place to look things up. You are \emph{not} meant to read this before the lessons: the lessons teach reading through real words, introducing each letter as a word needs it. This page just gathers the system in one spot.

\section*{How Devanagari works (the three facts the lessons teach)}

\begin{enumerate}
\raggedright
\setlength{\itemsep}{0.35em}
  \item \textbf{Consonants carry a built-in \textquotedblleft{}a\textquotedblright{}.} \hi{क} = \textquotedblleft{}ka,\textquotedblright{} \hi{न} = \textquotedblleft{}na,\textquotedblright{} \hi{म} = \textquotedblleft{}ma.\textquotedblright{} You never write the short \emph{a} — it's already there.
  \item \textbf{A vowel sign (\emph{mātrā}) changes that built-in vowel.} Attached to a consonant, it swaps the \emph{a} for another vowel: \textbf{\hi{ा}} = ā (\hi{का} = kā) · \textbf{\hi{ि}} = i (\hi{कि} = ki, written \emph{before}, read \emph{after}) · \textbf{\hi{ी}} = ī · \textbf{\hi{ु}} = u · \textbf{\hi{ू}} = ū · \textbf{\hi{े}} = e (\hi{के} = ke) · \textbf{\hi{ै}} = ai · \textbf{\hi{ो}} = o · \textbf{\hi{ौ}} = au.
  \item \textbf{A \emph{halant} (\hi{्}) removes the built-in vowel.} \hi{क्} = bare \textquotedblleft{}k.\textquotedblright{} A vowel-less consonant leans onto the next, forming a \textbf{conjunct}: \hi{स्} + \hi{त} $\to$ \hi{स्त} (\textquotedblleft{}st\textquotedblright{}), \hi{न्} + \hi{य} $\to$ \hi{न्य} (\textquotedblleft{}ny\textquotedblright{}), \hi{क्} + \hi{र} $\to$ \hi{क्र} (\textquotedblleft{}kr\textquotedblright{}).
\end{enumerate}

\section*{Independent vowels (word-initial)}

When a word \emph{starts} with a vowel (no consonant to attach to), a full vowel letter is used: \textbf{\hi{अ}} a · \textbf{\hi{आ}} ā · \textbf{\hi{इ}} i · \textbf{\hi{ई}} ī · \textbf{\hi{उ}} u · \textbf{\hi{ऊ}} ū · \textbf{\hi{ए}} e · \textbf{\hi{ऐ}} ai · \textbf{\hi{ओ}} o · \textbf{\hi{औ}} au.

\section*{Sounds worth flagging}

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
\setlength{\itemsep}{0.35em}
  \item \textbf{Aspirated vs. plain} consonants are different letters and change meaning: \hi{क} k / \hi{ख} kh, \hi{ग} g / \hi{घ} gh, \hi{त} t / \hi{थ} th, \hi{द} d / \hi{ध} dh, \hi{प} p / \hi{फ} ph, etc. The \textquotedblleft{}h\textquotedblright{} is a real puff of breath.
  \item \textbf{Retroflex} consonants (\hi{ट} ṭ, \hi{ड} ḍ, \hi{ण} ṇ, etc.) are made with the tongue curled back — distinct from the dental \hi{त}/\hi{द} (tongue on the teeth).
  \item \textbf{Nasalization}: a dot (anusvāra \hi{ं}) or moon-dot (candrabindu \hi{ँ}) nasalizes the vowel.
  \item \textbf{Nukta letters} (a dot under a letter) mark sounds borrowed mostly from Persian/Arabic/English: \hi{क़} q, \hi{ख़} x/kh, \hi{ग़} ġ, \hi{ज़} z, \hi{फ़} f, \hi{ड़}/\hi{ढ़} retroflex flaps.
\end{itemize}

\section*{The two vocabularies}

Not pronunciation, but the key to Hindi: many everyday ideas have \textbf{two} words — a \textbf{Sanskrit} (\emph{tatsama}) one, often formal/literary, and a \textbf{Perso-Arabic} one, often everyday: \emph{dhanyavād} / \emph{shukriyā} (\textquotedblleft{}thanks\textquotedblright{}), \emph{namaste} / \emph{alvidā}. The lessons trace which is which.
